column4: Goldman Sachs is under pressure. So is the rest of Wall Street.
column10: [Goldman Sachs (GS) CEO David Solomon acknowledged a series of negative headlines about his company when he spoke to shareholders during an investor day in late February."I hate the noise," Solomon said bluntly, adding that "I wish the noise was different."That noise is just as loud five months later.The most storied name on Wall Street is under a microscope as it fights to maintain its crown as the world's top dealmaker. It is wrestling with everything from job cuts and a global investment banking slump to reports of partner unrest and concerns about strategy.Even Solomon’s side gig as a DJ and his partial interest in a real estate company are subjects of scrutiny.Goldman spokesman Tony Fratto said Solomon "and the entire leadership team are focused on delivering for clients and executing on our strategy" and that the CEO has acted as a DJ at "only a handful of events a year - and hasn’t in over a year."As for any dissension among the partners, he said "the reality is people can have disagreements" and that’s "normal."Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon. (AP Photo/Patrick Semansky) (ASSOCIATED PRESS)Goldman is not the only big name on Wall Street under pressure.Firms with big investment banking and trading units have made or announced cuts of roughly 12,000 jobs since the end of 2022. Dealmaking is drying up amid a rise in interest rates, economic uncertainty and the failures of several sizable regional banks.Those cutting back include other Wall Street stalwarts such as Morgan Stanley (MS), Citigroup (C) and JPMorgan Chase (JPM).UBS, which also has a sizable presence on Wall Street, reportedly plans to cut 35,000 jobs at former rival Credit Suisse Group AG following an emergency takeover orchestrated by the Swiss government in March.These challenges are a reminder that the pain for the banking industry is still acute months after the failures of regional lenders Silicon Valley Bank, Signature Bank and First Republic. And the giant banks that rely on mergers or IPO underwriting for sizable portions of their revenue have specific problems of their own.Story continues'Green shoots'The slowdown in dealmaking will come into sharper focus in a few weeks when the biggest institutions report their second-quarter results.Worldwide revenue from mergers and acquisitions for the first half of 2023 fell 38% compared to the same period last year, according to data from Refinitiv, amounting to the slowest first half for deal making since 2020.That follows a subpar first quarter when major banks advising on mergers or IPO underwriting reported sizable drops in fee revenue. The largest decrease of 26% belonged to Goldman. A hint at the possible results came this week when a smaller investment bank, Jefferies Financial Group (JEF), said its fiscal second-quarter revenue from investment banking plunged 26%, pulling down profit for the period.One bright spot, however, was that capital markets net revenue surged 30% to $543 million in the quarter. Jefferies also said that “the month of June has brought green shoots.”Many big banks have warned that trading revenue will also be down in the second quarter. That includes Goldman. Its chief operating officer, John Waldron, has said such revenue may fall 25%.Goldman is fighting this year to keep its title as the world's largest dealmaker. It was still ahead of rival JPMorgan through June 30, according to Dealogic, with a market share lead of 1%. Another data provider, Refinitiv, said Goldman trailed JPMorgan as of June 27.Winning 'cures all'It wasn't long ago that deal making was responsible for helping Goldman — and the rest of Wall Street — churn out record profits.The last boom came in 2021, when CEOs used surging markets as a reason to buy other companies, go public, or take on new debt. Through the period, Goldman Sachs dramatically outperformed rival firms, scoring its best year of revenue in its century and a half historyThen came a year that most of Wall Street would like to forget.In 2022, three major stock averages fell by the most since 2008 and bonds had their worst year on record. Inflation reached its highest level in four decades, triggering an aggressive series of interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve.All of that new economic uncertainty curbed the optimism needed from the corporate clients that are the lifeblood of Wall Street's investment banking business. As a result, bonuses were slashed and jobs were cut.John Waldron, chief operating officer of Goldman Sachs. REUTERS/Brendan McDermid (Brendan McDermid / reuters)Goldman recorded its second-highest annual revenue that year but it had a rough end to 2022, with profits down a whopping 69% in the final quarter amid a sharp decline in deal-making. In January of this year Goldman Sachs let go of roughly 3,000 employees, or 6% of its workforce.Solomon, facing shareholders at the end of February during the firm's second-ever investor day, admitted mistakes were made. "I think we’ve accomplished a lot over the past few years. We got some things right, got some things wrong."He dismissed chatter about mass partner exits, saying there were fewer partner transitions in 2022 than any other year going back to 2014.He also made it clear Goldman would be scaling back its prior ambitions to become a consumer banking giant (a project known as Marcus) and would instead look to lean more heavily on the steady, fee-generating business of wealth management. Goldman has sold some Marcus loans and will likely take a write down for a purchase of a fintech lender."The culture of Goldman Sachs is incredibly strong," Solomon said on Feb. 28.Less than two weeks later Goldman found itself in the middle of another controversial situation when it tried to help Silicon Valley Bank raise capital while purchasing some of its securities. The events preceded a run on the regional bank that upended the banking world.Silicon Valley Bank was seized by regulators on March 10. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu, File) (ASSOCIATED PRESS)A spokesman said Goldman informed Silicon Valley Bank in writing that it would not act as its adviser on the securities sale and recommended the bank hire a third-party financial adviser for that transaction. Federal officials are now reportedly investigating the role Goldman played in those final days.Devin Ryan, analyst for JMP Securities with an overweight rating on Goldman, predicted the firm would bounce back once markets and dealmaking recovers.“Goldman Sachs will disproportionately benefit when that happens," he told Yahoo Finance.Winning, said Wells Fargo banking analyst Mike Mayo, "cures all.""So if and when capital markets resume," he added, paychecks will go higher and "I think employees will be a lot happier.”Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column4: Earnings: 'Banks can set the tone,' says strategist
column10: [How can investors prepare for the upcoming earnings season? Michele Schneider, Marketgauge.com Chief Strategist, joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss big banks setting the tone for earnings, as well as what to expect from AI stocks, consumer-facing companies, airlines, oil, and gas.Video Transcript[AUDIO LOGO]DIANE KING HALL: A new earnings season just around the corner. And as usual, big banks like JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, and Citigroup will kick off the busy quarter next week.But Wall Street's biggest banks might be facing tighter profit margins following the aftermath of the banking crisis and collapse of Silicon Valley Bank back in March.Now some analysts are painting a gloomy picture for this quarter, saying Q2 is expected to be the third consecutive quarter of declining S&P 500 earnings. Michele Schneider, MarketGauge.com Chief Strategist is still here with us. So Michele, do you agree with that assessment?MICHELE SCHNEIDER: Well, if we look at what had boosted the bank earnings in the past, a lot of it was from their financial side, right? From people-- from people being involved in investments and that liquidity that it added to banks.And also being able to borrow money, which right now is much more difficult that these higher interest rates. And even though the housing market has been strong, obviously mortgage applications have been impacted by rising rates.So yeah, at this point, I would think that for this quarter, we will not necessarily see very strong bank earnings. And you mentioned the banking crisis. I mean, some people feel that it was just a little bit too soon in terms of saying crisis over. I mean, what did it last? Like about four days.And so the higher the interest rates go, that could put a lot of squeeze particularly on the commercial real estate and the regional bank side. So I would not have great high expectations at this point.BRAD SMITH: Do you think there's a theme that emerges this earnings season? It seemed like last earnings season, it was all about how can we say AI in various amount of ways for companies who had no business saying it in some of them. So Michele, is there one theme that you believe will emerge this earnings season?Story continuesMICHELE SCHNEIDER: Well, again, I think that you have-- the advantage is going to be to any of these companies that have managed to survive throughout the first six months because of their operating cash flow. And that has given them some level of growth.And that's why you have to mention AI, right? Because that certainly has happened there. So that's kind of what I would continue to look at. I mean, just take Nike in terms of the consumer space, right? Earnings not great and Nike stock has been falling.So if that's any kind of foreshadowing, that means that we will see a lot of stress in terms of the earnings. And it's going to be, of course, what they say about future as we get through the rest of the year.And at this point, right now, with the expectations of two more interest rate hikes and as we've talked about already, inflation not necessarily being in control, at least in the places that affect consumers the worst, yeah, I would think that we'll see AI probably still do well.Apple, all these companies as they continue to compete with one another. But a lot of the other companies not necessarily doing so great.DIANE KING HALL: So can you name more of those companies, besides Nike, that where you expect to see some stress. Would these be consumer company-- consumer-facing companies or where are you expecting to see this stress?MICHELE SCHNEIDER: Well, we started with banks so I think the banks can set the tone for sure. And if they do not come in great or worse than expected, right?I mean, the thing with earnings seasons, first of all, is that it's always looking backwards and it's really about what the actual number is versus the expectation that has the greatest impact to the market. And even that is, sometimes, a short-term impact. So the longer term impact generally is what they project going forward, the guidance.And so, yeah, I mean-- I mean, like, let's take some of the high flyers in terms of the consumer space that we've seen in the past, Lululemon being one. I think that those kind of companies could actually start to feel the strain.Whereas some of the fast food companies that had had stress could actually start to come back a little bit. You know, like a McDonald's, for example.So I think that that's really-- you have to think what's going to be if everything we've just talked about, Diane, turns out to be true. If the market has seen a top. If the yields are going to have to be stretched. If we are going to enter more stagflation, potentially recession as we get into 2024.Where are these company-- where are people are going to spend their money? And they're going to spend the money on more of the staples, which did terribly, right? I mean Target, of course, had its own reasons for doing that outside of being Staples, which went down against discretionary. But that could rebound.A company like Walmart could continue to do well. You know, where people are going to go and buy cheapest goods they can get at this point.BRAD SMITH: Michele, just lastly while we're on this topic. One of my favorite conversations to kick off the earnings season is with Delta's executives.Because it gives us a sense of where this counter-cyclical recovery that we've heard about from travel companies is continuing or what type of consumer profile they're continuing to engage with.Particularly across services spending right now in the experience economy, are you expecting for there to be any slowdown within that?MICHELE SCHNEIDER: Well, it's such a good question, Brad, because we actually were in the cruise line stocks and had taken some profits along the way.And I've talked to people who do go on a lot of cruises. They said they're booked out for at least the next year. And so again, at this point, that still could be an outperforming area as people seem to be cutting back in certain things but yet wanting to get out, wanting to get away, wanting to go on a cruise, wanting to get on a plane.Do I think that can be impacted? Of course. As we know, when things get sour, if they go sour, it's really hard for anything, particularly in this more sort of discretionary area, to sustain.And then we have this other kind of crazy thing going on which is the possibility of labor unrest as wages continue to have to increase to keep up. And you know, you had a strike right now in UPS and I think it's still out there. And there's been threats of airline strikes.So I think I wouldn't necessarily be all that overly optimistic anywhere when it comes to the equity space, even in the airlines and the cruise lines.DIANE KING HALL: Interesting. So maybe some caution ahead. All right, Michele Schneider, thank you so much. We appreciate you for joining us today. Michele Schneider, MarketGauge.com Chief Strategist.MICHELE SCHNEIDER: Thank you.]

column4: Goldman and JPMorgan duke it out for the title of top M&A advisor for the first half of 2023
column10: [Nowhere are bragging rights more hotly contested than on Wall Street. And for the first six months of 2023 Goldman Sachs kept the crown as the top M&A advisor globally, according to new data from both Dealogic and Refinitiv.Goldman worked on 145 deals valued at $321.3 billion during the first six months of this year, Dealogic said. In second place was JPMorgan with $309.9 billion in transactions, while BofA Securities jumped up a spot to third place with $228.7 billion in deals. Refinitiv data had Goldman in first with $305.6 billion worth of deals, while JPMorgan placed second with $301.5 billion, and Morgan Stanley ranked third with $193 billion in mergers. BofA was fourth with $192.8 billion in transactions, said Refinitiv, an LSEG (London Stock Exchange Group) business.Goldman and JPMorgan declined to comment.Bloomberg, using its own data, reported last week that Goldman had lost its crown as the top global M&A advisor for the first time in five years, tumbling to second place in the league table rankings with $237 billion worth of transactions. JPMorgan was the lead M&A advisor this year with $284 billion in deals, the story said.Investment banks typically use league tables as a marketing tool to attract new clients.For the layperson, league tables don’t really mean too much. But on Wall Street, it can be contentious. In April, Refinitiv had JPMorgan edging out Goldman Sachs for the top spot at the end of the first quarter. Dealogic had it the other way around, Reuters reported. This caused Goldman to ask Refinitiv for an explanation while JPMorgan quizzed Dealogic, the story said. Refinitiv and Dealogic will typically provide data with slight differences, but it’s rare for them to have different winners of the most coveted spot in the league tables. Dealogic told Reuters that its methodology is based on feedback from the market, while Refinitiv said it had a process in place that couldn’t be unduly influenced.Story continuesOtherwise, the slowdown in mergers continued during the first half of 2023. The number of global announced M&A transactions dropped by 21% as of July 3, while valuations plunged by 39%, Dealogic said. So far in 2023, there were 18,311 global announced deals, valued at $1.36 trillion. This compares to 23,247 mergers totaling $2.24 trillion for the same time period last year. The drop in deals is the slowest since the pandemic of 2020 caused dealmaking to go on pause for several months.The biggest deal so far this year is Pfizer’s $45.6 billion buy of cancer specialist Seagen. Glencore’s nearly $32 billion offer for Teck Resources’ steelmaking core business came in second while a SPAC merger, Black Spade Acquisition’s $23 billion combination with VinFast Auto, ranked third.When it comes to private equity, the number of global deals fell by 30% to 1,309. But valuation plunged by about 61% to $314.6 billion. In the U.S., the results were just as bad. The number of U.S. private equity deals fell by 33% to 519 transactions valued at $168.5 billion, a 59% drop. The biggest global PE deal was Bunge, the grains merchant that is backed by Glencore, which agreed to buy Viterra, a Canadian grain handling business, in June. column4: Earnings: 'Banks can set the tone,' says strategist
column10: [How can investors prepare for the upcoming earnings season? Michele Schneider, Marketgauge.com Chief Strategist, joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss big banks setting the tone for earnings, as well as what to expect from AI stocks, consumer-facing companies, airlines, oil, and gas.Video Transcript[AUDIO LOGO]DIANE KING HALL: A new earnings season just around the corner. And as usual, big banks like JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, and Citigroup will kick off the busy quarter next week.But Wall Street's biggest banks might be facing tighter profit margins following the aftermath of the banking crisis and collapse of Silicon Valley Bank back in March.Now some analysts are painting a gloomy picture for this quarter, saying Q2 is expected to be the third consecutive quarter of declining S&P 500 earnings. Michele Schneider, MarketGauge.com Chief Strategist is still here with us. So Michele, do you agree with that assessment?MICHELE SCHNEIDER: Well, if we look at what had boosted the bank earnings in the past, a lot of it was from their financial side, right? From people-- from people being involved in investments and that liquidity that it added to banks.And also being able to borrow money, which right now is much more difficult that these higher interest rates. And even though the housing market has been strong, obviously mortgage applications have been impacted by rising rates.So yeah, at this point, I would think that for this quarter, we will not necessarily see very strong bank earnings. And you mentioned the banking crisis. I mean, some people feel that it was just a little bit too soon in terms of saying crisis over. I mean, what did it last? Like about four days.And so the higher the interest rates go, that could put a lot of squeeze particularly on the commercial real estate and the regional bank side. So I would not have great high expectations at this point.BRAD SMITH: Do you think there's a theme that emerges this earnings season? It seemed like last earnings season, it was all about how can we say AI in various amount of ways for companies who had no business saying it in some of them. So Michele, is there one theme that you believe will emerge this earnings season?Story continuesMICHELE SCHNEIDER: Well, again, I think that you have-- the advantage is going to be to any of these companies that have managed to survive throughout the first six months because of their operating cash flow. And that has given them some level of growth.And that's why you have to mention AI, right? Because that certainly has happened there. So that's kind of what I would continue to look at. I mean, just take Nike in terms of the consumer space, right? Earnings not great and Nike stock has been falling.So if that's any kind of foreshadowing, that means that we will see a lot of stress in terms of the earnings. And it's going to be, of course, what they say about future as we get through the rest of the year.And at this point, right now, with the expectations of two more interest rate hikes and as we've talked about already, inflation not necessarily being in control, at least in the places that affect consumers the worst, yeah, I would think that we'll see AI probably still do well.Apple, all these companies as they continue to compete with one another. But a lot of the other companies not necessarily doing so great.DIANE KING HALL: So can you name more of those companies, besides Nike, that where you expect to see some stress. Would these be consumer company-- consumer-facing companies or where are you expecting to see this stress?MICHELE SCHNEIDER: Well, we started with banks so I think the banks can set the tone for sure. And if they do not come in great or worse than expected, right?I mean, the thing with earnings seasons, first of all, is that it's always looking backwards and it's really about what the actual number is versus the expectation that has the greatest impact to the market. And even that is, sometimes, a short-term impact. So the longer term impact generally is what they project going forward, the guidance.And so, yeah, I mean-- I mean, like, let's take some of the high flyers in terms of the consumer space that we've seen in the past, Lululemon being one. I think that those kind of companies could actually start to feel the strain.Whereas some of the fast food companies that had had stress could actually start to come back a little bit. You know, like a McDonald's, for example.So I think that that's really-- you have to think what's going to be if everything we've just talked about, Diane, turns out to be true. If the market has seen a top. If the yields are going to have to be stretched. If we are going to enter more stagflation, potentially recession as we get into 2024.Where are these company-- where are people are going to spend their money? And they're going to spend the money on more of the staples, which did terribly, right? I mean Target, of course, had its own reasons for doing that outside of being Staples, which went down against discretionary. But that could rebound.A company like Walmart could continue to do well. You know, where people are going to go and buy cheapest goods they can get at this point.BRAD SMITH: Michele, just lastly while we're on this topic. One of my favorite conversations to kick off the earnings season is with Delta's executives.Because it gives us a sense of where this counter-cyclical recovery that we've heard about from travel companies is continuing or what type of consumer profile they're continuing to engage with.Particularly across services spending right now in the experience economy, are you expecting for there to be any slowdown within that?MICHELE SCHNEIDER: Well, it's such a good question, Brad, because we actually were in the cruise line stocks and had taken some profits along the way.And I've talked to people who do go on a lot of cruises. They said they're booked out for at least the next year. And so again, at this point, that still could be an outperforming area as people seem to be cutting back in certain things but yet wanting to get out, wanting to get away, wanting to go on a cruise, wanting to get on a plane.Do I think that can be impacted? Of course. As we know, when things get sour, if they go sour, it's really hard for anything, particularly in this more sort of discretionary area, to sustain.And then we have this other kind of crazy thing going on which is the possibility of labor unrest as wages continue to have to increase to keep up. And you know, you had a strike right now in UPS and I think it's still out there. And there's been threats of airline strikes.So I think I wouldn't necessarily be all that overly optimistic anywhere when it comes to the equity space, even in the airlines and the cruise lines.DIANE KING HALL: Interesting. So maybe some caution ahead. All right, Michele Schneider, thank you so much. We appreciate you for joining us today. Michele Schneider, MarketGauge.com Chief Strategist.MICHELE SCHNEIDER: Thank you.]

column4: Goldman and JPMorgan duke it out for the title of top M&A advisor for the first half of 2023
column10: [Nowhere are bragging rights more hotly contested than on Wall Street. And for the first six months of 2023 Goldman Sachs kept the crown as the top M&A advisor globally, according to new data from both Dealogic and Refinitiv.Goldman worked on 145 deals valued at $321.3 billion during the first six months of this year, Dealogic said. In second place was JPMorgan with $309.9 billion in transactions, while BofA Securities jumped up a spot to third place with $228.7 billion in deals. Refinitiv data had Goldman in first with $305.6 billion worth of deals, while JPMorgan placed second with $301.5 billion, and Morgan Stanley ranked third with $193 billion in mergers. BofA was fourth with $192.8 billion in transactions, said Refinitiv, an LSEG (London Stock Exchange Group) business.Goldman and JPMorgan declined to comment.Bloomberg, using its own data, reported last week that Goldman had lost its crown as the top global M&A advisor for the first time in five years, tumbling to second place in the league table rankings with $237 billion worth of transactions. JPMorgan was the lead M&A advisor this year with $284 billion in deals, the story said.Investment banks typically use league tables as a marketing tool to attract new clients.For the layperson, league tables don’t really mean too much. But on Wall Street, it can be contentious. In April, Refinitiv had JPMorgan edging out Goldman Sachs for the top spot at the end of the first quarter. Dealogic had it the other way around, Reuters reported. This caused Goldman to ask Refinitiv for an explanation while JPMorgan quizzed Dealogic, the story said. Refinitiv and Dealogic will typically provide data with slight differences, but it’s rare for them to have different winners of the most coveted spot in the league tables. Dealogic told Reuters that its methodology is based on feedback from the market, while Refinitiv said it had a process in place that couldn’t be unduly influenced.Story continuesOtherwise, the slowdown in mergers continued during the first half of 2023. The number of global announced M&A transactions dropped by 21% as of July 3, while valuations plunged by 39%, Dealogic said. So far in 2023, there were 18,311 global announced deals, valued at $1.36 trillion. This compares to 23,247 mergers totaling $2.24 trillion for the same time period last year. The drop in deals is the slowest since the pandemic of 2020 caused dealmaking to go on pause for several months.The biggest deal so far this year is Pfizer’s $45.6 billion buy of cancer specialist Seagen. Glencore’s nearly $32 billion offer for Teck Resources’ steelmaking core business came in second while a SPAC merger, Black Spade Acquisition’s $23 billion combination with VinFast Auto, ranked third.When it comes to private equity, the number of global deals fell by 30% to 1,309. But valuation plunged by about 61% to $314.6 billion. In the U.S., the results were just as bad. The number of U.S. private equity deals fell by 33% to 519 transactions valued at $168.5 billion, a 59% drop. The biggest global PE deal was Bunge, the grains merchant that is backed by Glencore, which agreed to buy Viterra, a Canadian grain handling business, in June. Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and British Columbia Investment Management Corp both own stakes in Viterra.And now for this month's cartoon from Ian Foley...See you tomorrow,Luisa BeltranTwitter: @LuisaRBeltranEmail: luisa.beltran@fortune.comSubmit a deal for the Term Sheet newsletter here.Jackson Fordyce curated the deals section of today’s newsletter.This story was originally featured on Fortune.comMore from Fortune: 5 side hustles where you may earn over $20,000 per year—all while working from homeLooking to make extra cash? column4: Goldman and JPMorgan duke it out for the title of top M&A advisor for the first half of 2023
column10: [Nowhere are bragging rights more hotly contested than on Wall Street. And for the first six months of 2023 Goldman Sachs kept the crown as the top M&A advisor globally, according to new data from both Dealogic and Refinitiv.Goldman worked on 145 deals valued at $321.3 billion during the first six months of this year, Dealogic said. In second place was JPMorgan with $309.9 billion in transactions, while BofA Securities jumped up a spot to third place with $228.7 billion in deals. Refinitiv data had Goldman in first with $305.6 billion worth of deals, while JPMorgan placed second with $301.5 billion, and Morgan Stanley ranked third with $193 billion in mergers. BofA was fourth with $192.8 billion in transactions, said Refinitiv, an LSEG (London Stock Exchange Group) business.Goldman and JPMorgan declined to comment.Bloomberg, using its own data, reported last week that Goldman had lost its crown as the top global M&A advisor for the first time in five years, tumbling to second place in the league table rankings with $237 billion worth of transactions. JPMorgan was the lead M&A advisor this year with $284 billion in deals, the story said.Investment banks typically use league tables as a marketing tool to attract new clients.For the layperson, league tables don’t really mean too much. But on Wall Street, it can be contentious. In April, Refinitiv had JPMorgan edging out Goldman Sachs for the top spot at the end of the first quarter. Dealogic had it the other way around, Reuters reported. This caused Goldman to ask Refinitiv for an explanation while JPMorgan quizzed Dealogic, the story said. Refinitiv and Dealogic will typically provide data with slight differences, but it’s rare for them to have different winners of the most coveted spot in the league tables. Dealogic told Reuters that its methodology is based on feedback from the market, while Refinitiv said it had a process in place that couldn’t be unduly influenced.Story continuesOtherwise, the slowdown in mergers continued during the first half of 2023. The number of global announced M&A transactions dropped by 21% as of July 3, while valuations plunged by 39%, Dealogic said. So far in 2023, there were 18,311 global announced deals, valued at $1.36 trillion. This compares to 23,247 mergers totaling $2.24 trillion for the same time period last year. The drop in deals is the slowest since the pandemic of 2020 caused dealmaking to go on pause for several months.The biggest deal so far this year is Pfizer’s $45.6 billion buy of cancer specialist Seagen. Glencore’s nearly $32 billion offer for Teck Resources’ steelmaking core business came in second while a SPAC merger, Black Spade Acquisition’s $23 billion combination with VinFast Auto, ranked third.When it comes to private equity, the number of global deals fell by 30% to 1,309. But valuation plunged by about 61% to $314.6 billion. In the U.S., the results were just as bad. The number of U.S. private equity deals fell by 33% to 519 transactions valued at $168.5 billion, a 59% drop. The biggest global PE deal was Bunge, the grains merchant that is backed by Glencore, which agreed to buy Viterra, a Canadian grain handling business, in June. Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and British Columbia Investment Management Corp both own stakes in Viterra.And now for this month's cartoon from Ian Foley...See you tomorrow,Luisa BeltranTwitter: @LuisaRBeltranEmail: luisa.beltran@fortune.comSubmit a deal for the Term Sheet newsletter here.Jackson Fordyce curated the deals section of today’s newsletter.This story was originally featured on Fortune.comMore from Fortune: 5 side hustles where you may earn over $20,000 per year—all while working from homeLooking to make extra cash? column4: Bank earnings: Headwinds to watch out for
column10: [Big banks will start reporting their quarterly results on Friday, with JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo on tap. Stephen Biggar, Director of Financial Services Research at Argus Research, tells Yahoo Finance what is he expecting to hear from banks this quarter.Video TranscriptSEANA SMITH: Tougher capital rules for US banks proposed by the Fed's Barr isn't the only thing that investors are closely watching. Earnings season is just around the corner. And the nation's largest banks are gearing up to report their quarterly results. Here with more on what we can expect, we want to bring in Stephen Biggar, Director of Financial Services Research for Argus Research.Stephen, it's good to see you. So certainly, a challenging set up here for the banks, a higher interest rate environment. We have also the possibility here of stricter regulations. And the implications of that is something that investors are waiting to see. How does this set us up for this round of earnings season?STEPHEN BIGGAR: Yeah, so, well, I think it's going to be, you know, not banks' finest hour in terms of earnings this quarter. Clearly, the higher rate environment that was very helpful in 2022 for net interest margins is having a detrimental effect now. You've got slowing loan growth, just less demand as you have much higher interest rates here. And that's the intended effect of the Federal Reserve.Net interest margins, it looks like they peaked in the fourth quarter of last year. We're likely to see additional pressure sequentially on margins as deposit rates have really increased quite a bit here as banks try to stay competitive with a lot of higher-yielding alternatives out there. And then, of course, on the other bit of lending, the business would be loss provisions.And, you know, we're starting to see some increased delinquencies, particularly in the credit card and auto lending market. So I think banks are going to be conservative here, add to loan loss provisions. And all in all, of course, all three of those will dampen earnings growth a little bit for the quarter.Story continuesAKIKO FUJITA: So you talk about the growth we're likely to see in loan losses, defaults in credit card payments. But we've heard repeatedly about the potential cliff waiting, especially in commercial real estate. What are you going to be looking for, at least in this quarter, in terms of the potential rising risk on that front for banks?STEPHEN BIGGAR: Yeah, definitely, the commercial real estate does, you know, loom as a potential problem area. And we've seen some defaults already kind of pick up there. You know, I think banks did a very good job in the first quarter of laying out the risks there.Typically, for the very large banks, commercial real estate is about 10% of their loan book. Commercial and the office space in particular, which is where a lot of the damage is and the higher delinquency rates, is typically more like, you know, 3% to 4%. It's quite a bit higher, about double that, at the regional bank level, but still, you know, manageable at this point.And of course, the underwriting standards have been better in commercial real estate than they were 5 or 10 or 15 years ago. So that's beneficial for banks. They have generally about a 40-- or 60, I should say, 60% loan to value in there. And, you know, that gives them a fair amount of leeway should these go south.But clearly, a lot of refinancings are coming due in the commercial real estate space over the next three years and definitely among the highest problem areas that we're watching in terms of delinquencies and credit quality.SEANA SMITH: Stephen, we know a lot of the focus in past earnings season most recently have been on guidance. We've already seen a number of the banks, specifically the regionals, already lower their guidance. M&T Bank was one of those names that already lowered their forecast. Do you think we'll see further cuts here over the next several weeks?STEPHEN BIGGAR: Well, I would say, I mean, given that we have earnings coming out at the end of the week, banks have gone into a quiet period. We're probably not going to see additional drop here. A lot of that softer guidance came out during some of the conferences they had at the investment bank. So I think we're, you know, sort of set for the quarter here now that the quarter has ended.But, you know, I think the commentary and the guidance on the earnings calls that we get is probably not going to be a barn burner either, right? We're probably going to, you know, see more of the same banks sort of coming into the last quarter. Actually, some of them were expecting that the Fed would have been done raising interest rates, you know, by mid-year.That looks not to be the case as you look three months later now. Some had expected even a cut by the end of the year. That seems very much off the table now. So I think we're stuck with these higher rates, which will, again, dampen lending growth and slow the economy further, which is bad for credit quality.AKIKO FUJITA: Stephen, it's still a big concern that the regional lenders, the medium-sized banks-- we have seen in the spring, there was, like, JPMorgan swallowing up First Republic. I mean, when you look at the financial space right now, are you expecting more consolidation, you know, not necessarily failed banks, but just seeing where the banks are, especially the medium-sized banks, and the impact they're continuing to take from higher rates?STEPHEN BIGGAR: Yeah, I think-- and, you know, we've seen some support at the regulatory level. There might be some appetite for additional consolidation. I think, you know, most would say it's safe to say we're overbanked in the US. Particularly relative to other countries, we've got about 4,700 FDIC-insured commercial banks in the US today.They all can't make it, I would say, in this environment. I think it, you know, behooves most of them to take a look at partnerships and outright acquisitions if they can't do it themselves. That's tough for a bank, obviously, that wants to maintain its independence, you know, they feel they have the right product set for their local markets, and so forth.But the regulatory aspects here, what happens with the new-- particularly the regulations that are going to be put in place, it's going to make it very hard for banks to compete, for banks to continually elevate. You know, we know that capital cushions only go in one direction, right? And that's up. So they continually have to add more to the capital.Even as they grow larger, you would say it's counterintuitive that the larger banks have to set aside even more. But it doesn't make them safer. It makes them, you know, less prone to failure, certainly, and looks better in the eye of the regulators. So I think we'll see more consolidation here. I don't think we're going to have the number of banks over the next five or 10 years, but I think there's a lot of consolidation that needs to take place.SEANA SMITH: And, Stephen, what is the timeline of that consolidation? Is it something that's going to take years to play out?STEPHEN BIGGAR: Yeah, absolutely. I don't think we're-- you know, banks can only take on so much at a time. The large banks, when they do acquisitions that are sizable, I would say, about 1/3 of their asset base or higher, they tend to take about a year and a half to do that before they even can look at something even more significant. Smaller size or sort of token acquisitions that are in the same service territory, that makes sense. Maybe they can do that a little faster.But yeah, we're talking years here and not just a couple of quarters, obviously. You know, it took about 20 years for banks to have the number of banks that we have in the US. And it's probably going to take another 20, unless we get some, you know, very favorable regulatory environment that actually encourages consolidation. And I don't see that happening.SEANA SMITH: So, Stephen, given all this, given the very challenging sort of backdrop that we're in right now, who is best positioned in this environment?STEPHEN BIGGAR: Well, it'll still favor of the large banks, the JPMorgans, Bank of Americas, even Morgan Stanley, and some of the super regionals, I would say, like the Truist Financial, PNC Financial, U.S. Bancorp. These are banks that have already largely met the-- or can more easily meet the higher capital requirements. It will take them a matter of quarters, let's say, to no more than two years to reach these higher capital levels that are most likely to be in place.And we do expect, of course, the banks to sail through this year's stress test. The CICA results came in, but those are going to get more stringent going forward. We're going to have a scenario where interest rates spike over the forecast period versus decline, which has been the way it's worked with stress tests in the past.The Basel III international regulations are going to get more strict and severe as well. They're going to add a couple of more nuances to scenarios and what happens with banks, in particular about risk weighted assets and trading assets as well. So that will affect the Morgan Stanley's and Goldman Sachs of the world in particular. So I think those are still well positioned.Banks in the kind of $100 billion to $250 billion range or even $50 on their way to $100 billion are really going to have, you know, a tougher time. So I'd stick with the larger banks. They've got great earnings potential here. They're well diversified. They've got good yields at this point.And of course, many of these have suffered in the decline. They're well underperforming the market at this point. And that'll create some opportunities for investors.SEANA SMITH: All right, well, we'll start seeing these quarterly results later on this week. Stephen Biggar of Argus Research, thank you so much.STEPHEN BIGGAR: Thank you.]

column4: Earnings: 'Banks can set the tone,' says strategist
column10: [How can investors prepare for the upcoming earnings season? Michele Schneider, Marketgauge.com Chief Strategist, joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss big banks setting the tone for earnings, as well as what to expect from AI stocks, consumer-facing companies, airlines, oil, and gas.Video Transcript[AUDIO LOGO]DIANE KING HALL: A new earnings season just around the corner. And as usual, big banks like JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, and Citigroup will kick off the busy quarter next week.But Wall Street's biggest banks might be facing tighter profit margins following the aftermath of the banking crisis and collapse of Silicon Valley Bank back in March.Now some analysts are painting a gloomy picture for this quarter, saying Q2 is expected to be the third consecutive quarter of declining S&P 500 earnings. Michele Schneider, MarketGauge.com Chief Strategist is still here with us. So Michele, do you agree with that assessment?MICHELE SCHNEIDER: Well, if we look at what had boosted the bank earnings in the past, a lot of it was from their financial side, right? From people-- from people being involved in investments and that liquidity that it added to banks.And also being able to borrow money, which right now is much more difficult that these higher interest rates. And even though the housing market has been strong, obviously mortgage applications have been impacted by rising rates.So yeah, at this point, I would think that for this quarter, we will not necessarily see very strong bank earnings. And you mentioned the banking crisis. I mean, some people feel that it was just a little bit too soon in terms of saying crisis over. I mean, what did it last? Like about four days.And so the higher the interest rates go, that could put a lot of squeeze particularly on the commercial real estate and the regional bank side. So I would not have great high expectations at this point.BRAD SMITH: Do you think there's a theme that emerges this earnings season? It seemed like last earnings season, it was all about how can we say AI in various amount of ways for companies who had no business saying it in some of them. So Michele, is there one theme that you believe will emerge this earnings season?Story continuesMICHELE SCHNEIDER: Well, again, I think that you have-- the advantage is going to be to any of these companies that have managed to survive throughout the first six months because of their operating cash flow. And that has given them some level of growth.And that's why you have to mention AI, right? Because that certainly has happened there. So that's kind of what I would continue to look at. I mean, just take Nike in terms of the consumer space, right? Earnings not great and Nike stock has been falling.So if that's any kind of foreshadowing, that means that we will see a lot of stress in terms of the earnings. And it's going to be, of course, what they say about future as we get through the rest of the year.And at this point, right now, with the expectations of two more interest rate hikes and as we've talked about already, inflation not necessarily being in control, at least in the places that affect consumers the worst, yeah, I would think that we'll see AI probably still do well.Apple, all these companies as they continue to compete with one another. But a lot of the other companies not necessarily doing so great.DIANE KING HALL: So can you name more of those companies, besides Nike, that where you expect to see some stress. Would these be consumer company-- consumer-facing companies or where are you expecting to see this stress?MICHELE SCHNEIDER: Well, we started with banks so I think the banks can set the tone for sure. And if they do not come in great or worse than expected, right?I mean, the thing with earnings seasons, first of all, is that it's always looking backwards and it's really about what the actual number is versus the expectation that has the greatest impact to the market. And even that is, sometimes, a short-term impact. So the longer term impact generally is what they project going forward, the guidance.And so, yeah, I mean-- I mean, like, let's take some of the high flyers in terms of the consumer space that we've seen in the past, Lululemon being one. I think that those kind of companies could actually start to feel the strain.Whereas some of the fast food companies that had had stress could actually start to come back a little bit. You know, like a McDonald's, for example.So I think that that's really-- you have to think what's going to be if everything we've just talked about, Diane, turns out to be true. If the market has seen a top. If the yields are going to have to be stretched. If we are going to enter more stagflation, potentially recession as we get into 2024.Where are these company-- where are people are going to spend their money? And they're going to spend the money on more of the staples, which did terribly, right? I mean Target, of course, had its own reasons for doing that outside of being Staples, which went down against discretionary. But that could rebound.A company like Walmart could continue to do well. You know, where people are going to go and buy cheapest goods they can get at this point.BRAD SMITH: Michele, just lastly while we're on this topic. One of my favorite conversations to kick off the earnings season is with Delta's executives.Because it gives us a sense of where this counter-cyclical recovery that we've heard about from travel companies is continuing or what type of consumer profile they're continuing to engage with.Particularly across services spending right now in the experience economy, are you expecting for there to be any slowdown within that?MICHELE SCHNEIDER: Well, it's such a good question, Brad, because we actually were in the cruise line stocks and had taken some profits along the way.And I've talked to people who do go on a lot of cruises. They said they're booked out for at least the next year. And so again, at this point, that still could be an outperforming area as people seem to be cutting back in certain things but yet wanting to get out, wanting to get away, wanting to go on a cruise, wanting to get on a plane.Do I think that can be impacted? Of course. As we know, when things get sour, if they go sour, it's really hard for anything, particularly in this more sort of discretionary area, to sustain.And then we have this other kind of crazy thing going on which is the possibility of labor unrest as wages continue to have to increase to keep up. And you know, you had a strike right now in UPS and I think it's still out there. And there's been threats of airline strikes.So I think I wouldn't necessarily be all that overly optimistic anywhere when it comes to the equity space, even in the airlines and the cruise lines.DIANE KING HALL: Interesting. So maybe some caution ahead. All right, Michele Schneider, thank you so much. We appreciate you for joining us today. Michele Schneider, MarketGauge.com Chief Strategist.MICHELE SCHNEIDER: Thank you.]

column4: Banks are fighting to keep deposits. How much is it costing them?
column10: [Bank deposit rates are the highest in a decade and a half. That’s good news for savers, but bad news for lenders as they prepare to release their second-quarter results.US banks spent the last several months competing with each other to keep or bring back depositors following the turmoil that took down three sizable regional institutions and triggered outflows across the banking system.That scramble pushed rates on savings accounts to 5.05% at the end of the second quarter, according to Bankrate, their steepest level since February 2008.Read more: The best high-yield savings account rates for July 2023The challenge for banks across the US is that these higher funding costs are eating into a key measure of profitability known as net interest margin, which measures the difference between what lenders make from their loans and what they pay for their deposits.That will likely act as a drag on results for some banks in the quarter, especially the mid-sized regional institutions that ran into trouble last spring, while reducing estimates of what they can earn for the rest of the year.“The surprises this quarter will be for the banks that do not lower expectations,” Wells Fargo bank analyst Mike Mayo told Yahoo Finance.Banks, added Argus Research's Stephen Biggar, "have a deposit conundrum."'Green shoots'?These pressures will be at the front of mind for investors starting Friday as they digest the first set of second quarter earnings from JPMorgan Chase (JPM), Citigroup (C), Wells Fargo (WFC), and State Street (STT).Bank of America (BAC) and Morgan Stanley (MS) report next Tuesday and Goldman Sachs (GS) next Wednesday. A slew of other regional banks will also report in the coming weeks.Some of the biggest US banks are expected to once again demonstrate their resilience and diversity, showing they can continue to charge more for their loans while leaning on their sprawling franchises to generate additional revenue.Story continuesJPMorgan, Wells Fargo, and Bank of America are all expected to show jumps in net income when compared to the year-earlier period, according to analyst estimates, while Citigroup, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley are expected to report profit declines.JPMorgan's headquarters in New York City. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig, File) (ASSOCIATED PRESS)Those that are more dependent on investment banking, such as Goldman, are expected to be particularly challenged by a recent drought in deal making.Global investment banking revenues for the second quarter fell by 8% from the first quarter and 52% from a year ago, according to Dealogic. However, the business improved through the second half of the quarter, prompting some observers to predict “green shoots” ahead.“I’m turning to believing investment banking will not have great earnings but they’re going to be surprising, and I think better than expected,” said Dick Bove, a bank analyst with Odeon Capital.Investors will also be watching to see whether many of these big banks increase the amounts they set aside for future loan losses, a sign that they expect the US economy and credit conditions to worsen.“We're starting to see some increased delinquencies, particularly in the credit card and auto lending market,” said Biggar, Argus Research's director of financial services.'A huge amount of problems'Smaller regional banks are clearly not under the same amount of pressure as they were in March, when the fall of Silicon Valley Bank triggered panic across the country.But they still “face a huge amount of problems,” Bove said.The core issue is an aggressive campaign by the Federal Reserve to bring down inflation with higher interest rates. That campaign is lowering the value of the assets banks hold, such as bonds, while deposit costs creep higher and loan demand slows.Read more: Why now is a good time to open a savings account“We view accelerating deposit costs, not accelerating deposit outflows, as the most significant headwind to earnings for the next several quarters,“ Manan Gosalia, a regional bank analyst for Morgan Stanley, said in a research note.Higher rates have traditionally worked to the advantage of banks since it allows them to charge more for their loans than their deposits.But the panic of the spring “has changed the calculus a bit” for some banks, the Fed’s vice chair of supervision Michael Barr said Monday. Some lenders “are now paying up more for deposits,” and the Fed is “paying careful attention to that.”Silicon Valley Bank was seized on March 10. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu, File) (ASSOCIATED PRESS)The Fed has made it clear that more hikes are coming this year. Regulators are also preparing new capital requirements for banks with more than $100 billion in assets that will force some to hold greater buffers against losses. That will increase the stability of those lenders but will also make it even more difficult to earn robust profits in the near term.Many banks have already warned at a conference in June that their net interest margins are going to drop by more than they expected for the quarter or the year, including executives for US Bancorp (USB), Citizens Financial Group (CFG), Comerica (CMA), Huntington (HBAN), KeyCorp (KEY), and Zions (ZION).“I’ve only been a banker for 10 years, so I haven’t seen a time when we’ve needed deposits as an industry as much as we do now,” Darrin Williams, the CEO of the 58-branch Southern Bancorp, told Yahoo Finance.The amount Southern Bancorp is paying customers has risen 600% since the Fed’s interest rate hiking cycle began, Williams added.“Our cost of funds continues to rise just because our customers demand that.”The larger banks aren’t immune to some of these same challenges.“Deposits will continue the trend of being slightly down from here,” Jennifer Piepszak, co-CEO of JPMorgan Chase's massive consumer and community bank, said at a conference in June.The bank has predicted it will earn net interest income of $84 billion in 2023, but if the deposit pressure keeps up, that figure could experience a “mild reprice,” she said.Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column4: Bank earnings: Headwinds to watch out for
column10: [Big banks will start reporting their quarterly results on Friday, with JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo on tap. Stephen Biggar, Director of Financial Services Research at Argus Research, tells Yahoo Finance what is he expecting to hear from banks this quarter.Video TranscriptSEANA SMITH: Tougher capital rules for US banks proposed by the Fed's Barr isn't the only thing that investors are closely watching. Earnings season is just around the corner. And the nation's largest banks are gearing up to report their quarterly results. Here with more on what we can expect, we want to bring in Stephen Biggar, Director of Financial Services Research for Argus Research.Stephen, it's good to see you. So certainly, a challenging set up here for the banks, a higher interest rate environment. We have also the possibility here of stricter regulations. And the implications of that is something that investors are waiting to see. How does this set us up for this round of earnings season?STEPHEN BIGGAR: Yeah, so, well, I think it's going to be, you know, not banks' finest hour in terms of earnings this quarter. Clearly, the higher rate environment that was very helpful in 2022 for net interest margins is having a detrimental effect now. You've got slowing loan growth, just less demand as you have much higher interest rates here. And that's the intended effect of the Federal Reserve.Net interest margins, it looks like they peaked in the fourth quarter of last year. We're likely to see additional pressure sequentially on margins as deposit rates have really increased quite a bit here as banks try to stay competitive with a lot of higher-yielding alternatives out there. And then, of course, on the other bit of lending, the business would be loss provisions.And, you know, we're starting to see some increased delinquencies, particularly in the credit card and auto lending market. So I think banks are going to be conservative here, add to loan loss provisions. And all in all, of course, all three of those will dampen earnings growth a little bit for the quarter.Story continuesAKIKO FUJITA: So you talk about the growth we're likely to see in loan losses, defaults in credit card payments. But we've heard repeatedly about the potential cliff waiting, especially in commercial real estate. What are you going to be looking for, at least in this quarter, in terms of the potential rising risk on that front for banks?STEPHEN BIGGAR: Yeah, definitely, the commercial real estate does, you know, loom as a potential problem area. And we've seen some defaults already kind of pick up there. You know, I think banks did a very good job in the first quarter of laying out the risks there.Typically, for the very large banks, commercial real estate is about 10% of their loan book. Commercial and the office space in particular, which is where a lot of the damage is and the higher delinquency rates, is typically more like, you know, 3% to 4%. It's quite a bit higher, about double that, at the regional bank level, but still, you know, manageable at this point.And of course, the underwriting standards have been better in commercial real estate than they were 5 or 10 or 15 years ago. So that's beneficial for banks. They have generally about a 40-- or 60, I should say, 60% loan to value in there. And, you know, that gives them a fair amount of leeway should these go south.But clearly, a lot of refinancings are coming due in the commercial real estate space over the next three years and definitely among the highest problem areas that we're watching in terms of delinquencies and credit quality.SEANA SMITH: Stephen, we know a lot of the focus in past earnings season most recently have been on guidance. We've already seen a number of the banks, specifically the regionals, already lower their guidance. M&T Bank was one of those names that already lowered their forecast. Do you think we'll see further cuts here over the next several weeks?STEPHEN BIGGAR: Well, I would say, I mean, given that we have earnings coming out at the end of the week, banks have gone into a quiet period. We're probably not going to see additional drop here. A lot of that softer guidance came out during some of the conferences they had at the investment bank. So I think we're, you know, sort of set for the quarter here now that the quarter has ended.But, you know, I think the commentary and the guidance on the earnings calls that we get is probably not going to be a barn burner either, right? We're probably going to, you know, see more of the same banks sort of coming into the last quarter. Actually, some of them were expecting that the Fed would have been done raising interest rates, you know, by mid-year.That looks not to be the case as you look three months later now. Some had expected even a cut by the end of the year. That seems very much off the table now. So I think we're stuck with these higher rates, which will, again, dampen lending growth and slow the economy further, which is bad for credit quality.AKIKO FUJITA: Stephen, it's still a big concern that the regional lenders, the medium-sized banks-- we have seen in the spring, there was, like, JPMorgan swallowing up First Republic. I mean, when you look at the financial space right now, are you expecting more consolidation, you know, not necessarily failed banks, but just seeing where the banks are, especially the medium-sized banks, and the impact they're continuing to take from higher rates?STEPHEN BIGGAR: Yeah, I think-- and, you know, we've seen some support at the regulatory level. There might be some appetite for additional consolidation. I think, you know, most would say it's safe to say we're overbanked in the US. Particularly relative to other countries, we've got about 4,700 FDIC-insured commercial banks in the US today.They all can't make it, I would say, in this environment. I think it, you know, behooves most of them to take a look at partnerships and outright acquisitions if they can't do it themselves. That's tough for a bank, obviously, that wants to maintain its independence, you know, they feel they have the right product set for their local markets, and so forth.But the regulatory aspects here, what happens with the new-- particularly the regulations that are going to be put in place, it's going to make it very hard for banks to compete, for banks to continually elevate. You know, we know that capital cushions only go in one direction, right? And that's up. So they continually have to add more to the capital.Even as they grow larger, you would say it's counterintuitive that the larger banks have to set aside even more. But it doesn't make them safer. It makes them, you know, less prone to failure, certainly, and looks better in the eye of the regulators. So I think we'll see more consolidation here. I don't think we're going to have the number of banks over the next five or 10 years, but I think there's a lot of consolidation that needs to take place.SEANA SMITH: And, Stephen, what is the timeline of that consolidation? Is it something that's going to take years to play out?STEPHEN BIGGAR: Yeah, absolutely. I don't think we're-- you know, banks can only take on so much at a time. The large banks, when they do acquisitions that are sizable, I would say, about 1/3 of their asset base or higher, they tend to take about a year and a half to do that before they even can look at something even more significant. Smaller size or sort of token acquisitions that are in the same service territory, that makes sense. Maybe they can do that a little faster.But yeah, we're talking years here and not just a couple of quarters, obviously. You know, it took about 20 years for banks to have the number of banks that we have in the US. And it's probably going to take another 20, unless we get some, you know, very favorable regulatory environment that actually encourages consolidation. And I don't see that happening.SEANA SMITH: So, Stephen, given all this, given the very challenging sort of backdrop that we're in right now, who is best positioned in this environment?STEPHEN BIGGAR: Well, it'll still favor of the large banks, the JPMorgans, Bank of Americas, even Morgan Stanley, and some of the super regionals, I would say, like the Truist Financial, PNC Financial, U.S. Bancorp. These are banks that have already largely met the-- or can more easily meet the higher capital requirements. It will take them a matter of quarters, let's say, to no more than two years to reach these higher capital levels that are most likely to be in place.And we do expect, of course, the banks to sail through this year's stress test. The CICA results came in, but those are going to get more stringent going forward. We're going to have a scenario where interest rates spike over the forecast period versus decline, which has been the way it's worked with stress tests in the past.The Basel III international regulations are going to get more strict and severe as well. They're going to add a couple of more nuances to scenarios and what happens with banks, in particular about risk weighted assets and trading assets as well. So that will affect the Morgan Stanley's and Goldman Sachs of the world in particular. So I think those are still well positioned.Banks in the kind of $100 billion to $250 billion range or even $50 on their way to $100 billion are really going to have, you know, a tougher time. So I'd stick with the larger banks. They've got great earnings potential here. They're well diversified. They've got good yields at this point.And of course, many of these have suffered in the decline. They're well underperforming the market at this point. And that'll create some opportunities for investors.SEANA SMITH: All right, well, we'll start seeing these quarterly results later on this week. Stephen Biggar of Argus Research, thank you so much.STEPHEN BIGGAR: Thank you.]

column10: [The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. GS is slated to release second-quarter 2023 earnings on Jul 19, before market open. Price and EPS Surprise The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. Price and EPS SurpriseThe Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. price-eps-surprise | The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. QuoteMajor Factors at PlayTrading Revenues: At an industry conference,Goldman Sachs’president and chief operating officer, John Waldron, revealed that the firm expected trading revenues to decline 25% year over year in second-quarter 2023. "The macro backdrop is extraordinarily challenging,” he added. This led to sluggish capital market activity, and muted equities and fixed-income activity levels than that witnessed a year ago.Tougher comps from the prior year are also expected to have weighed on the company’s year-over-year performance in second-quarter 2023. column4: Banks are fighting to keep deposits. At what cost?
column10: [Bank deposit rates are the highest in a decade and a half. That’s good news for savers, but bad news for lenders as they prepare to release their second-quarter results.US banks spent the last several months competing with each other to keep or bring back depositors following the turmoil that took down three sizable regional institutions and triggered outflows across the banking system.That scramble pushed rates on savings accounts to 5.05% at the end of the second quarter, according to Bankrate, their steepest level since February 2008.Read more: The best high-yield savings account rates for July 2023The challenge for banks across the US is that these higher funding costs are eating into a key measure of profitability known as net interest margin, which measures the difference between what lenders make from their loans and what they pay for their deposits.That will likely act as a drag on results for some banks in the quarter, especially the mid-sized regional institutions that ran into trouble last spring, while reducing estimates of what they can earn for the rest of the year.“The surprises this quarter will be for the banks that do not lower expectations,” Wells Fargo bank analyst Mike Mayo told Yahoo Finance.Banks, added Argus Research's Stephen Biggar, "have a deposit conundrum."'Green shoots'?These pressures will be at the front of mind for investors starting Friday as they digest the first set of second quarter earnings from JPMorgan Chase (JPM), Citigroup (C), Wells Fargo (WFC), and State Street (STT).Bank of America (BAC) and Morgan Stanley (MS) report next Tuesday and Goldman Sachs (GS) next Wednesday. A slew of other regional banks will also report in the coming weeks.Some of the biggest US banks are expected to once again demonstrate their resilience and diversity, showing they can continue to charge more for their loans while leaning on their sprawling franchises to generate additional revenue.Story continuesJPMorgan, Wells Fargo, and Bank of America are all expected to show jumps in net income when compared to the year-earlier period, according to analyst estimates, while Citigroup, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley are expected to report profit declines.JPMorgan's headquarters in New York City. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig, File) (ASSOCIATED PRESS)Those that are more dependent on investment banking, such as Goldman, are expected to be particularly challenged by a recent drought in deal making.Global investment banking revenues for the second quarter fell by 8% from the first quarter and 52% from a year ago, according to Dealogic. However, the business improved through the second half of the quarter, prompting some observers to predict “green shoots” ahead.“I’m turning to believing investment banking will not have great earnings but they’re going to be surprising, and I think better than expected,” said Dick Bove, a bank analyst with Odeon Capital.Investors will also be watching to see whether many of these big banks increase the amounts they set aside for future loan losses, a sign that they expect the US economy and credit conditions to worsen.“We're starting to see some increased delinquencies, particularly in the credit card and auto lending market,” said Biggar, Argus Research's director of financial services.'A huge amount of problems'Smaller regional banks are clearly not under the same amount of pressure as they were in March, when the fall of Silicon Valley Bank triggered panic across the country.But they still “face a huge amount of problems,” Bove said.The core issue is an aggressive campaign by the Federal Reserve to bring down inflation with higher interest rates. That campaign is lowering the value of the assets banks hold, such as bonds, while deposit costs creep higher and loan demand slows.Read more: Why now is a good time to open a savings account“We view accelerating deposit costs, not accelerating deposit outflows, as the most significant headwind to earnings for the next several quarters,“ Manan Gosalia, a regional bank analyst for Morgan Stanley, said in a research note.Higher rates have traditionally worked to the advantage of banks since it allows them to charge more for their loans than their deposits.But the panic of the spring “has changed the calculus a bit” for some banks, the Fed’s vice chair of supervision Michael Barr said Monday. Some lenders “are now paying up more for deposits,” and the Fed is “paying careful attention to that.”Silicon Valley Bank was seized on March 10. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu, File) (ASSOCIATED PRESS)The Fed has made it clear that more hikes are coming this year. Regulators are also preparing new capital requirements for banks with more than $100 billion in assets that will force some to hold greater buffers against losses. That will increase the stability of those lenders but will also make it even more difficult to earn robust profits in the near term.Many banks have already warned at a conference in June that their net interest margins are going to drop by more than they expected for the quarter or the year, including executives for US Bancorp (USB), Citizens Financial Group (CFG), Comerica (CMA), Huntington (HBAN), KeyCorp (KEY), and Zions (ZION).“I’ve only been a banker for 10 years, so I haven’t seen a time when we’ve needed deposits as an industry as much as we do now,” Darrin Williams, the CEO of the 58-branch Southern Bancorp, told Yahoo Finance.The amount Southern Bancorp is paying customers has risen 600% since the Fed’s interest rate hiking cycle began, Williams added.“Our cost of funds continues to rise just because our customers demand that.”The larger banks aren’t immune to some of these same challenges.“Deposits will continue the trend of being slightly down from here,” Jennifer Piepszak, co-CEO of JPMorgan Chase's massive consumer and community bank, said at a conference in June.The bank has predicted it will earn net interest income of $84 billion in 2023, but if the deposit pressure keeps up, that figure could experience a “mild reprice,” she said.Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]
